title: Version 3 measures, alerts and dashboards the Workbench as one; the target architecture is 19 services
source: 05 Technical architecture/Recovery Workbench Observability and Monitoring Design v3.docx
description: Version 3 has one measure set, one Service health dashboard for 'Platform administrator, ACE team' and one instance of each alert for the whole Workbench. Architecture v5 gives 19 services, each with its own api and worker deployment, schema and login, topic rwb.<short>.events.v1 and task queue rwb-<short> (slides 33 and 41), and ADR-023 is 'Observability per service' (Rules v1 R8.4). No source fixes the name, the panel set, the refresh interval, the saved query or the per-service threshold of a per-service dashboard or alert, so the document can say what is measured per service but cannot fix the artefact.
evidence: v3 section 1 row 'Service' ('per endpoint'), section 2 rows 'Error rate' and 'Latency', section 3 row 'Service health' ('Platform administrator, ACE team'); Architecture v5 slides 33 ('api deployment and a worker deployment', KEDA on the task queue) and 41 (one topic and one task queue per service); Rules v1 R8.4 ADR-023.
owner_role: Solution architect with the platform team
proposed: Version 4 reads each measure and each alert with the service as the unit, gives the 19 measured units (1.1), the per-service reading of the 13 alerts (2.1) and one Service health dashboard per service (3.1), and leaves the dashboard name, the panel order, the refresh interval and the saved query to the baseline of RWB-PLT-N005-OPS.

title: No source names the owner of a per-service dashboard or alert rule as a team
source: 22 Microservice Realignment/Recovery Workbench Microservice Ownership Map v1.xlsx; 05 Technical architecture/Recovery Workbench Observability and Monitoring Design v3.docx
description: Version 3 names recipients as roles ('Platform administrator', 'Data steward', 'Team managers', 'Risk and model risk officer'), not as owners of a dashboard or an alert rule. The Ownership Map v1 Services sheet gives code, service, name, wave, schema, REST base, topic and queue for the 19 services and has no observability, on-call or dashboard column, and no row of its Rulings sheet covers a metric, a dashboard or an alert. Rules v1 R5.3 gives the fixed owner phrase by work type only, so who builds and runs a per-service dashboard and alert rule is not settled by any source.
evidence: Ownership Map v1 Services sheet (8 columns, 19 rows) and Rulings sheet (no observability row); v3 section 2 column 'Goes to' and section 3 column 'For'; Rules v1 R5.3 ('DevOps team (suggested; any team may pick up this story)' for OPS).
owner_role: Platform team with the DevOps team
proposed: The owner of a per-service dashboard, alert rule and run book is the service code of the Ownership Map v1, with the DevOps team as the suggested owner of the work under Rules v1 R5.3; the baseline is built by RWB-PLT-N005-OPS in wave 0 and each service adds its own panels.

title: Metric and span names, labels, retention, sampling and the alert delivery channel are not specified
source: 05 Technical architecture/Recovery Workbench Observability and Monitoring Design v3.docx; 22 Microservice Realignment/Recovery Workbench Architecture v5 Text Extract v1.md
description: Version 3 names the tools only (Log Analytics, Prometheus, Grafana, OpenTelemetry per Architecture v5 slides 8 and 49). No source gives the metric or span names, the label set that would carry the service, the retention of metrics, logs and traces, the sampling policy, the alert delivery channel or the suppression window. A per-service read needs the service label on every metric; the sources do not name it.
evidence: v3 section 1 column 'Source' (Log Analytics, Prometheus, 'Drools runtime metrics in Prometheus'); v3 section 3 paragraph (Grafana fed by Prometheus); Architecture v5 slides 8 and 35 (observability, OpenTelemetry, one trace) and 49 (OpenTelemetry, W3C Trace Context).
proposed: The metric, span and label conventions, the retention and sampling values and the alert delivery channel are published in the platform baseline RWB-PLT-N005-OPS before wave 1; this document fixes only the panels and the thresholds it inherits from version 3.

title: The Jobs row still reads the Quartz job table, which the target architecture retires
source: 05 Technical architecture/Recovery Workbench Observability and Monitoring Design v3.docx; 22 Microservice Realignment/Recovery Workbench Architecture v5 Text Extract v1.md
description: Version 3 measures job runs, duration and missed runs from the Quartz job table. Architecture v5 retires the shared Quartz and batch tables: each job is a Temporal Schedule or an event-started workflow in the owning service, JOB-05 is retired because the timers are durable timers inside the workflow, and the job map gives one owner per job (slide 44; DP-10; ADR-016). The Quartz table therefore has no rows to measure.
evidence: v3 section 1 row 'Jobs' ('Quartz job table'); Architecture v5 slide 44 (job map with the mechanism per job, 'JOB-05 Timer check ... durable timers (retired)', 'The ACE shared Quartz and batch tables are no longer used by Recovery'); Rules v1 R5.5 DP-10.
owner_role: Platform team with the DevOps team
proposed: Version 4 reads the Jobs row as the Temporal Schedules and event-started workflows of the owning service, with the job map of Architecture v5 slide 44 as the owner list and the job catalogue of P2 rwb-integration as the register.

title: The decision log is now written locally by each service and sealed centrally
source: 05 Technical architecture/Recovery Workbench Observability and Monitoring Design v3.docx; 22 Microservice Realignment/Recovery Workbench Architecture v5 Text Extract v1.md
description: Version 3 measures one decision log (entries a day, write failures, chain check result). Architecture v5 changes the model: each service writes the decision record in its own schema in the same transaction as the change, hash-linked to its previous record, and rwb-decision collects rwb.decision-record.v1 into the central ledger within 5 minutes, with the daily chain check as JOB-14 at 02:00 (slide 28; ADR-022; DP-03). One 'write failures' count and one 'chain check result' no longer describe the system.
evidence: v3 section 1 row 'Decision log' and section 2 rows 'Decision log write failed' and 'Hash chain break'; Architecture v5 slide 28 (local record, chain, central collection within 5 minutes, daily seal) and slide 44 JOB-14 (owner rwb-decision, Schedule 02:00); Rules v1 R5.5 DP-03.
owner_role: Solution architect with Risk and Internal Audit
proposed: Version 4 measures the local decision record of each service and the central ledger of P7 rwb-decision as two instances of the same two alerts, with the chain check read per service and once for the ledger.

title: The alert recipient roles of version 3 are not mapped to role codes in rwb-access
source: 05 Technical architecture/Recovery Workbench Observability and Monitoring Design v3.docx; 22 Microservice Realignment/Recovery Workbench Microservice Ownership Map v1.xlsx
description: Version 3 sends alerts to 'Platform administrator', 'Data steward', 'Team managers', 'Risk and model risk officer', 'Compliance, internal audit' and 'Center of excellence analyst', and names only two role codes, RW-PLATADM and RW-COE, on the workflow dashboard row. rwb-access (P4) holds the Recovery roles as data, and the Ownership Map has no row that maps these six names to a role code. A per-service alert routed to a role therefore has no code to route to.
evidence: v3 section 2 column 'Goes to' and section 3 columns 'For' (rows 'Service health', 'Data health', 'Work health', 'Agent health', 'Workflow health (Grafana)'); Ownership Map v1 Tables sheet (role, permission, masking_rule, delegation_limit to P4) and Rulings sheet (no role-mapping row); Architecture v5 slide 41 P4 row ('Recovery roles as data').
proposed: The six recipient names are kept as they are and read as role names; the role codes are settled with the rwb-access role model before the per-service alert rules are built, and no code is invented here.

title: The rule package compile alert names P3 while the registry is P7 and the load happens in every owning service
source: 05 Technical architecture/Recovery Workbench Observability and Monitoring Design v3.docx; 22 Microservice Realignment/Recovery Workbench Architecture v5 Text Extract v1.md; 22 Microservice Realignment/Recovery Workbench Microservice Ownership Map v1.xlsx
description: Version 3 raises 'Rule package compile failed' on MSG-P3-027 with check compile and sends it to the center of excellence analyst and the platform administrator. In the target architecture the registry, the versions and the four-eyes approval are P7 rwb-decision, and each owning service loads the version in force, verifies the checksum and keeps the last good model on failure (Architecture v5 slide 27; ADR-017; DP-04). A compile failure therefore happens in the owning service, not in P3, while the message ID stays MSG-P3-027.
evidence: v3 section 2 row 'Rule package compile failed' and section 4 ('The rule package run book ... is owned by RWB-E1-073'); Architecture v5 slide 27 (governance central in rwb-decision, evaluation local, checksum, last good model) and slide 41; Ownership Map v1 Tables sheet (rule_package, rule_package_version, rule_row to P7); split_plan.json legacy RWB-E1-073 (slices in P3, P7, P6, P2).
owner_role: P7 rwb-decision with the centre of excellence
proposed: Version 4 keeps MSG-P3-027 character for character, raises the alert in the service that loads the package, names P7 rwb-decision as the registry owner and keeps RWB-E1-073 as the owner of the run book.

title: The Data health and Work health panels read objects of two services and the consoles are not named after the split
source: 05 Technical architecture/Recovery Workbench Observability and Monitoring Design v3.docx; 22 Microservice Realignment/Recovery Workbench Microservice Ownership Map v1.xlsx
description: Version 3 gives Data health to the data steward (loads, freshness, breaks, exceptions, from the data quality console) and Work health to team managers (queues, caps, breached service levels, exception queues). After the split the data products, the freshness and the reconciliation are P1 rwb-source-data and the queue measures are P3 rwb-case, and no source names a console for either. Which service serves a panel, and who owns the dashboard, is not settled.
evidence: v3 section 1 rows 'Data' ('Data quality console') and 'Cases' ('Workbench') and section 3 rows 'Data health' and 'Work health'; Ownership Map v1 Tables sheet (data_product, data_product_load, reconciliation_result to P1; queue_measure to P3).
owner_role: P1 rwb-source-data with P3 rwb-case and P9 rwb-reporting
proposed: Version 4 keeps the two dashboards and names the service behind each panel; the P1 freshness and reconciliation operations, the P3 queue measures and the P9 measures are the sources, and the console names of version 3 are kept as dashboard names only.

title: The hash chain check now spans 19 local chains and one central ledger
source: 05 Technical architecture/Recovery Workbench Observability and Monitoring Design v3.docx; 22 Microservice Realignment/Recovery Workbench Architecture v5 Text Extract v1.md
description: Version 3 measures one 'chain check result' and raises 'Hash chain break' when 'Daily check fails'. The target architecture has a hash-linked chain in each of the 19 services plus the central ledger in rwb-decision, checked daily by JOB-14 at 02:00. No source says whether the alert tests the 19 local chains, the ledger or both, how a break is attributed to a service, or what the counts mean when one chain is broken.
evidence: v3 section 1 row 'Decision log' ('chain check result') and section 2 row 'Hash chain break'; Architecture v5 slide 28 (each record linked to the one before; the chain checked every day) and slide 44 JOB-14 (owner rwb-decision, 02:00); 22 Microservice Realignment/Recovery Workbench Temporal and Drools Design Text Extract v1.md slide 16 (chain_seq, prev_hash, entry_hash; JOB-14 checks the chain at 02:00).
owner_role: P7 rwb-decision with Compliance and Internal Audit
proposed: Version 4 raises the alert on the local chain of each service and once on the central ledger, and attributes a break to the service whose chain fails; the run book of RWB-E1-073 and RWB-E2-037 names the check.
